explain.title: Ranks are levels of classification
explain.body: The groups into which organisms are classified are known as taxonomic ranks or taxa (singular “taxon”). The ranks form a hierarchy: each step down groups organisms more specifically.

explain.title: The Linnaean ranks
explain.body: Linnaeus suggested seven taxonomic ranks: kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus and species. Domain was added to this system in 1977 and is the highest rank.

explain.title: How the groups fit together
explain.body: A kingdom is divided into phyla or divisions; these are divided into classes, then orders, families and genera. Species is the lowest level of classification.

explain.title: Species
explain.body: It is the lowest level of classification. A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile (capable of reproduction) offspring.

explain.title: Use the plant term correctly
explain.body: For plants and fungi, use division in place of phylum. The other ranks keep the same order.

Forgetting that domain was added in 1977 and is higher than kingdom.

Some archaea live in extreme environments, whereas bacteria are found in all environments; many bacteria are beneficial decomposers.

explain.title: Domain Archaea
explain.body: These are the most primitive organisms on Earth. They are prokaryotes but their cell wall does not contain peptidoglycan but is made of various polypeptides and proteins. Their rRNA (ribosomal RNA) resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria. Their cell membrane contains unique lipids which enable them to live in extreme environments e.g., hot springs, salt lakes, and acidic or alkaline waters. However, they also exist in more common environments like soil and oceans.

explain.title: Domain Bacteria
explain.body: This domain contains bacteria and cyanobacteria. They are also prokaryotes. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan. They are found in all environments including soil, water, air, and in the bodies of organisms. They are unicellular. Many live solitary although some form chains, clusters, or colonies of cells.

explain.title: Domain Eukarya
explain.body: The domain includes all unicellular and multicellular eukaryotes. They have complex eukaryotic cells with nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. This domain contains kingdoms protista, fungi, plantae and animalia.

explain.title: Examples in Archaea
explain.body: Methanogens produce methane as a by-product of their metabolism. Halophiles are found in extremely salty environments. Thermophiles are found in hot springs. Acidophiles are found in extremely acidic environments.

Plant-like protists are autotrophs; animal-like protists are heterotrophs, and fungus-like protists absorb nutrients from decaying organic matter.
Kingdom Fungi consists of heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; they absorb food from decaying matter.
Kingdom Plantae includes multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose; they prepare food through photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it within their bodies; they have no cell walls.

explain.title: Protista
explain.body: Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular. Simple multicellular means that they do not have multicellular sex organs. explain.title: Fungi
explain.body: Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin. They absorb food from decaying matter in their surroundings rather than ingesting it. explain.title: Plantae

explain.title: Animalia
explain.body: Kingdom Animalia includes animals which are eukaryotic, multicellular and heterotrophic. They develop from embryos, ingest food and digest it within their bodies. Vertebrates and invertebrates are included in this kingdom.

notes.title: Biodiversity
notes.answer: Biodiversity is the variety of organisms in a particular area.
notes.explanation: Biodiversity describes the variety of organisms in a particular area. It is measured by counting the different kinds of organisms and considering the variation within each kind. Biodiversity is important because it supports ecosystem stability, helps regulate climate, provides natural resources, and supports industries.
notes.simple: Biodiversity means how many different kinds of living things live in a place, and how much they vary.

notes.title: Why do biologists classify organisms?
notes.answer: Classification is the process in which organisms are divided into groups and subgroups on the basis of similarities and differences found in them.
notes.explanation: Classification groups organisms by their similarities and differences. This makes them easier to study and helps biologists understand their relationships.
notes.simple: Classification is like sorting things into groups. Organisms with things in common are put together, so they are easier to study.
examples: Biologists can group organisms with similar physical characteristics together.
Genetic similarities and differences can help biologists understand similarities and differences in organisms’ structures and functions.
steps: Look for similarities and differences among organisms.
Use these features to place organisms into groups and subgroups.
Study the groups to identify organisms and understand their relationships.

notes.title: Taxonomic ranks: broad groups to specific groups
notes.answer: The highest rank is domain; the lowest rank is species.
notes.explanation: Taxonomic ranks arrange organisms in levels, from the broadest group, domain, to the most specific group, species. Each level is divided into smaller, related groups.
notes.simple: Think of classification as sorting organisms into groups that get smaller and more specific at each step.
examples: In the table in your textbook, a human belongs to the domain Eukarya and the species Homo sapiens.
For plants and fungi, the rank corresponding to phylum is called division.
steps: Start with the broadest rank: domain.
Move down through kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family and genus.
Finish with species, the lowest rank.

notes.title: History of Classification
notes.answer: Classification developed from two kingdoms to three kingdoms, then five kingdoms, and later three domains.
notes.explanation: Classification systems changed as scientists learned more about organisms. Aristotle grouped life into plants and animals. Later systems added kingdoms to deal with organisms that did not fit well, and Woese added domains above kingdoms.
notes.simple: Scientists changed the classification system as they learned more about how organisms are alike and different.
examples: Haeckel added Protista for Euglena-like organisms.
Woese divided organisms into the domains Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
steps: Remember the order: two kingdoms, three kingdoms, five kingdoms, then three domains.
Connect each system with its scientist: Aristotle, Haeckel, Whittaker and Woese.
Recall what changed: new groups were added to classify organisms more clearly.

notes.title: Three Domains of Living Organisms
notes.answer: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
notes.explanation: Living organisms are grouped into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes, but their cell walls differ. Eukarya includes organisms with cells that have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
notes.simple: Think of domains as the broadest groups of living organisms. Archaea and Bacteria have prokaryotic cells; Eukarya has eukaryotic cells.
steps: Remember the three names: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
For Archaea, remember that their cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan and some live in extreme environments.
For Bacteria, remember that their cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
For Eukarya, remember that its cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.

notes.answer: Viruses are acellular and lack the characteristics of the three domains of life, so they are not included in the classification system.
notes.explanation: Viruses are acellular particles at the borderline of living and non-living. They contain DNA or RNA inside a protein coat, cannot carry out metabolism, and need a host organism to make proteins and increase in number. They are not placed in the classification system because they lack the characteristics of the three domains of life. Prions consist only of protein, while viroids consist only of circular RNA.
notes.simple: A virus is not made of cells and cannot do everything a living organism does by itself. It must use a host to make more viruses, so it does not fit into the three-domain classification of life.
examples: A bacteriophage is a virus that attacks bacteria.
An influenza virus is another example of a virus.
steps: Check whether the particle is made of cells: viruses are acellular.
Check whether it can carry out metabolism: viruses cannot run metabolism.
Remember that viruses use a host to make proteins and increase in number.
Conclude that viruses lack the characteristics of the three domains of life, so they are not included in the classification system.
notes.checkQuestion: Why are viruses not included in the classification system?
notes.checkAnswer: They are acellular and lack the characteristics of the three domains of life.

notes.title: Binomial Nomenclature
notes.answer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of scientific naming in which each organism's name has two parts: its genus name followed by its species name.
notes.explanation: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-part scientific name. The first part names its genus and the second part names its species. This standard name is used worldwide, helping biologists communicate clearly even when they speak different languages.
notes.simple: Each organism gets a two-word scientific name: first its genus, then its species.
steps: Write the genus name first, beginning with a capital letter.
Write the species name second, beginning with a small letter.
Use italics when printing the scientific name.
If handwriting the name, underline its two parts separately.
notes.checkQuestion: In *Panthera tigris*, which word is the genus name?
notes.checkAnswer: The genus name comes first and begins with a capital letter; the species name comes second and begins with a small letter.

notes.title: Biodiversity and classification
notes.answer: The taxonomic ranks from broadest to most specific are Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
notes.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms. Biologists classify organisms into groups using shared features. The Linnaean ranks go from the broadest, domain, to the most specific, species. Scientific names use two words: genus followed by species.
notes.simple: Classification is like sorting living things into labelled groups, from very large groups down to very specific ones.
examples: Humans are named Homo sapiens: Homo is the genus and sapiens is the species.
The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
steps: Identify the organism’s features, such as its cell type and number of cells.
Use shared characteristics to place it in the correct domain and kingdom.
Continue through the taxonomic ranks from broad to specific.
Give the organism a two-word scientific name: genus first, species second.
notes.checkQuestion: Write the taxonomic ranks from broadest to most specific.
notes.checkAnswer: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

quiz.stem: Q2.5. Which of the following is a key characteristic that distinguishes eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells?

quiz.stem: Q2.6. Which kingdom includes organisms that are primarily unicellular, eukaryotic, and often heterotrophic?

quiz.stem: Q2.8. Why it is impossible to classify viruses within traditional biological kingdoms?
options: They lack cellular structure and organelles.
They are smaller in size than bacteria.

Many organisms that are classified in kingdoms cannot photosynthesise, so this is not the reason.
Being smaller than bacteria does not by itself prevent classification in a kingdom.
Parasitism alone does not prevent an organism from belonging to a kingdom.

quiz.stem: Q2.9. Which of the following is the correct way for writing the scientific name of humans?

quiz.stem: Q2.10. Which information you can get if you know the scientific name of an organism?

A scientific name gives genus and species, not phylum and genus.
The two parts of a scientific name identify the genus and species.

written.text: Q2.3. Describe the Linnaean system of classification in detail, stating the seven taxonomic ranks and their relationships.
modelAnswer: The Linnaean system classifies organisms in a hierarchy of nested groups.
From broadest to most specific, the seven ranks are Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
A broader rank contains one or more groups at the next, more specific rank.
Organisms become more similar and more closely related as we move from kingdom towards species.
Domain is also used as a broader rank above kingdom.

written.text: Q2.6. Discuss the challenges of classifying viruses within the traditional three domains of life.
modelAnswer: Viruses are acellular and lack the cellular structure and organelles found in organisms of the three domains.
They cannot carry out all life processes independently.
They reproduce only inside host cells.
For these reasons, viruses do not fit easily into the traditional three-domain classification of cellular life.
